extracted.intended_audience: essayists and satirical writers (contributors/readers of The Spectator)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing moral and satirical periodical essays: how to choose topics, how to treat vices and fashions, editorial limits (no private scandal or party embroilment), techniques for analysis of passions, and rules-of-thumb about translation/adaptation in musical/theatrical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address underlying causes not mere symptoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply remedies to the first seeds and principles of an affected dress, without descending to the dress itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foppish and fantastick ornaments are only indications of vice, not criminal in themselves. 'Extinguish Vanity in the Mind, and you naturally retrench the little Superfluities of Garniture and Equipage.' Attack the root (principles/habits) that give birth to outward extravagancies rather than merely ridiculing the trappings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirize vices in the abstract, not private individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not publish private intrigues or make examples of particular persons; consider crimes as they appear in a species, not as circumstanced in an individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper will not be a publisher of intrigues and cuckoldoms; if vices are exposed, they will be set upon in a body. Even when provoked, avoid singling out one offender — aim your stroke at a collective body of offenders to correct a class of vice rather than to defame individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid engaging in party politics or partisan quarrels
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep clear of everything that looks like taking a party side; do not inflame or increase feuds and animosities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although correspondents request notice of both sides, the essayist should remain an unconcerned Spectator and refrain from running into the outrages of a party. The goal is to allay public ferments, not to enrage them; neutrality preserves the paper's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer moral and human passions as subject matter over trivial fashion-complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper's intention is to enter into the passions of mankind and to correct depraved sentiments that give birth to little extravagancies in outward dress and behaviour, rather than to dwell only on red-heels or top-knots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foppish ornaments indicate vice but the essayist's focus should be on the principles producing them. Fashionable trifles can be used as examples, but the essay should aim to reveal and reform the underlying moral condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial policy: solicit harmless materials and help shape them
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reader has a hint they cannot pursue, a surprising story they don't know how to tell, or an example of epidemical vice or uncommon virtue, the editor will assist in working it up for public entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper promises assistance in converting correspondent materials into suitable essays; encourages submissions that furnish 'innocent Diversion' rather than private scandal or partisan attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base translations/adaptations chiefly on matching meter to tune
rubrics_metrics.description: Translators who make words of their own to have English verse answer the numbers of the Italian often destroy the sense — preserving metrics at the expense of meaning is bad practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: English lines made to fit Italian tunes can misplace emotional emphasis (soft notes aligning to 'Rage', etc.). The chief care should not be mechanical correspondence of syllabic numbers to tune when it alters sense; consider intelligibility and sense first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain intelligibility when adapting foreign performance traditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Performing an opera half in Italian and half in English (or wholly in a tongue the audience does not understand) produces a stage where dialogues are not comprehensible; avoid sacrificing comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practice of having some actors sing in Italian while others speak English led audiences to tire of 'understanding Half the Opera'; when adapting foreign forms, ensure the audience can follow or the art is undermined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical tone: attack systemic follies with humane severity (avoid petty spite)
rubrics_metrics.description: When exposing vice, aim at the collective, applying vigorous strokes ('I have so much of a Drawcansir in me, that I shall pass over a single Foe to charge whole Armies'), but temper cruelty with humanity in intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essayist may use strong satirical force against categories of wrongdoers (e.g., 'the Harlot and the Drunkard') but should avoid gratuitous private defamation; satire should be corrective rather than merely malicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a clear analytic structure when examining passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider a passion (such as envy) with relation to three heads: its Pains, its Reliefs, and its Happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tripartite method organizes the essay's exploration of an emotion: describe the suffering it causes (pains), the small consolations or partial mitigations (reliefs), and any illusory satisfactions (happiness). It is a rhetorical device for thorough moral analysis in an essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ self-deprecating humor and cheerfulness about defects
rubrics_metrics.description: When one has natural defects or oddnesses of aspect, it is best to be pleasant upon oneself; cheerful self-mockery disarms raillery and wins affection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: those with odd features who can 'jest upon himself' become liked by women and children. The Ugly Club plays this as a social strategy: members extol deformity humorously and elect by obvious grotesque traits — a model for using self-directed wit in writing and persona.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish true happiness from false (for character and moral portrayal)
rubrics_metrics.description: True happiness is retired, arises from enjoying oneself and a few select companions, loves shade and solitude; false happiness craves crowds, spectacle, and admiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this dichotomy when depicting characters or prescribing conduct: show how those seeking public admiration are dependent on spectators and thereby fragile, while those with private contentment are steady and virtuous. This is an aesthetic and moral criterion for character construction and thematic focus.
